display: PhD candidate in Chinese literature in Paris, translating late-Qing popular narrative into French.

signals.text: I'm looking for the ending of a late-Qing novella whose only surviving 1890s edition breaks off mid-sentence in chapter 18.
I don't know whether later editions or other complete copies of this novella exist anywhere, and I'd like to find out.
I've written to librarians in Shanghai and Taipei and had no answer. I'd welcome a way into collections in Beijing or elsewhere.
I'd like a second reader for hard classical passages, and for a reality check on my reading of the text.
I need a complete translation to attach as an appendix to my thesis, and my supervisor wants it finished.
I keep re-reading the same chapters trying to guess how the story ends. I'd like to talk with someone who knows the genre's conventions.
I'm preparing a conference abstract due on 20 October, and I'd like feedback on it.
My funding ends next summer, so I'm thinking about what comes after the PhD, whether that's finishing on time or teaching work.
My shared flat is breaking up in January and I need to find somewhere to live in Paris.
I'm worn down by the isolation of long library days and welcome any company around the work.
I'm learning a new tune for my jazz trio and would enjoy playing with other musicians.

offers.text: I read classical and modern Chinese fluently and have translated into French.
I have access to the university library, the BnF and the Inalco collections, and can check or request items there.
I keep a digital archive of scans and notes on late-Qing fiction that I can consult for others.
I co-authored a published article on serialised novels and know the late-Qing popular fiction literature.
I can compare print editions of Qing novellas and describe their bibliographic features.
I play upright or electric bass and have my own amp. I play weekly in a jazz trio at a small Paris bar.
I can write literary French translations of short Chinese texts, with notes for readers.
I can explain pawnshop motifs in Qing fiction, which is the subject of my thesis chapter.

catchers.hypo: I'm a librarian in Beijing. A reader asked about a late-Qing novella and I found a complete copy in our stacks. Is that of interest?
catchers.can: I'd send the title, the known text and a description of what's missing so you can check a match. I'd then work out how to obtain scans, with a grateful acknowledgement in the translation.
catchers.confirm: Does your copy include the last chapters, past chapter 18?

catchers.hypo: I collect old Chinese popular novels in Hong Kong. I own a later reprint of a story about a pawnshop and a stolen jade. Could that be what you're after?
catchers.can: I can compare your reprint to the text I have and say whether it's the same work and whether it continues past chapter 18.
catchers.confirm: Is the story set around a pawnshop with a stolen jade and a daughter?

catchers.hypo: I'm a scholar who has seen a serialised version of a novella like this in a newspaper from the 1890s. Would that help?
catchers.can: I'd gladly follow up. A newspaper serial could hold the ending, and I'd tell you what text to look for.
catchers.confirm: Was the serial run in the 1890s and does it reach a final chapter?

catchers.hypo: I'm a Chinese literature student in France and stuck on a classical passage in a Qing story. Could you read it with me?
catchers.can: I can read it with you, and my colleague Jin, a Chinese PhD student in my lab, often helps with tricky passages and may join.
catchers.confirm: Is the passage printed in standard type rather than a cursive manuscript hand?

catchers.hypo: I run a jazz night in Paris and my bassist just cancelled. Do you know someone who can sit in?
catchers.can: I can sit in myself on bass, and my trio's drummer Tom has great ears and could suggest other players.
catchers.confirm: Is the gig on a day other than Thursday, when I rehearse with my trio?

catchers.hypo: I edit a journal on Chinese literature. Do you have work on late-Qing popular narrative that could fit a special issue?
catchers.can: I can offer an article on pawnshop motifs in Qing fiction, and my supervisor, a senior professor in the field, may know suitable reviewers.
catchers.confirm: Is the journal open to work in progress from a PhD candidate?

catchers.hypo: I'm a publisher looking for a French translation of an obscure Chinese novella. Do you have anything?
catchers.can: I can show you a partial translation of 梅花当 and explain its place in late-Qing fiction. A full publication would depend on the ending.
catchers.confirm: Would you consider a partial text while we search for the ending?

forbids.text: I will not invent an ending for the novella. A reconstruction would have to be labelled as hypothesis.
I cannot travel to China without grants, so on-site archive visits are out unless someone funds them.
I do not read traditional-character cursive manuscripts easily, so I cannot take on that kind of transcription alone.
Thursday evenings are for my trio's rehearsal.

projects.name: French translation of 梅花当 (The Plum Blossom Pawnshop)
projects.text: A late-Qing novella from the 1890s. The translation stops at chapter 18 because the only known edition is missing its last pages. The preface says there are twenty-four chapters. The work needs the missing text.
roles_needed: librarian or archivist in China or Taiwan

policy.t1: Which novella I'm translating, what the surviving text is, and exactly where it breaks off.
policy.t2: My funding timeline and housing situation, once the other side is clearly a serious collaborator.
policy.never: Personal finances and details about my family.
